issues.legal_issue: A will is not proved to have been duly executed and attested when the evidence does not satisfactorily establish that the attesting witnesses saw the testator sign it and signed it in the testator’s presence.
material_facts: The will was relied on to claim title to property in proceedings concerning the estate.

The attesting witnesses said the will and a related deed were executed and attested at a registration office, but evidence accepted by the appellate court showed that the deed was executed and attested at the legal adviser’s house, where both witnesses were present.
The documents’ different inks, the witnesses’ account of the circumstances, and their inability to explain the ink evidence undermined their account of where execution and attestation occurred.
The attesting witnesses’ testimony was not sufficiently reliable to establish that they saw the testator sign the will and each signed it in the testator’s presence.
There was no other satisfactory evidence establishing due attestation.
issues.conclusion: The will was not proved to have been duly executed and attested and could not support the claimant’s title.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act requires attestation by two or more witnesses, each of whom must have seen the testator sign or received the specified acknowledgment, and each of whom must sign the will in the testator’s presence. The party relying on the will must establish compliance with those requirements through satisfactory evidence. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

predicates.claim_to_establish_title_under_a_will: A party relied on a will to establish title in a dispute over an estate.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_gave_an_unreliable_a: The witnesses who purported to attest the will gave an account of its execution that was undermined by other evidence and circumstances.
predicates.no_satisfactory_evidence_shows_the_requi: The evidence did not satisfactorily establish that the witnesses saw the testator sign the will and signed it in the testator’s presence.

issues.definition: When a party relies on a will for title, an unreliable account by its attesting witnesses and the absence of satisfactory evidence of the required signing and attestation mean the will is not proved as duly executed and attested.

issues.legal_issue: Signatures placed on a registration endorsement by persons identifying a testator do not, without evidence that they signed as attesting witnesses, prove due attestation of a will.
material_facts: The testator acknowledged execution of the will before a registrar.
Two persons who identified the testator signed beneath the registrar’s endorsement.
Neither identifier was called to testify about attesting the will, and the record did not establish that either signed in the capacity of an attesting witness.
issues.conclusion: The identifiers’ signatures on the registration endorsement did not prove due attestation of the will.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, attestation requires the prescribed witnessing and signing acts. A signature on a registration endorsement cannot simply be presumed to have been made animo attestandi, or in the capacity of an attesting witness. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act requires an attesting witness to be called to prove due execution and attestation. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

predicates.will_attestation_proof_dispute: A party disputed whether a will had been duly attested.
predicates.identifiers_signed_a_registration_endors: People who identified the testator signed beneath an endorsement made during registration of the will.
predicates.no_evidence_shows_they_signed_as_attesti: The evidence did not establish that those people signed with the intention of attesting the will.
predicates.identifiers_were_not_called_to_testify: Those people were not called as witnesses to prove that they attested the will.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a will’s attestation, signatures by identifiers on a registration endorsement, without evidence that they signed as attesting witnesses and without their testimony, do not by themselves prove due attestation.
